topics.title: Two empires and the Mediterranean world

learn.hook: Imagine one government ruling Spain, Egypt, Syria and England at the same time. For centuries, Rome did exactly that, with the Mediterranean Sea at its centre.
points: Between the birth of Christ and the early seventh century, two powerful empires dominated much of Europe, North Africa and West Asia (the Middle East): the Roman Empire and the Iranian empire, ruled first by the Parthians and then by the Sasanians.
The two were neighbours and frequent rivals, separated only by a narrow strip of land running along the river Euphrates.

The Mediterranean Sea was the heart of Rome's empire. Rome controlled all the territory around it: Spain and Italy in the west, Greece and Asia Minor (Turkey), Syria and Egypt in the east, and North Africa in the south.

Map work: the northern frontier ran along two great rivers, the Rhine and the Danube; the southern frontier was set by the Sahara desert. Within this vast space lived many peoples, languages and cultures.

example.q: Why do historians call the Roman world 'an empire across three continents'?
steps: List the regions around the Mediterranean that Rome controlled.
Spain, Italy, Gaul, Greece belong to Europe.
Syria, Asia Minor and Palestine belong to Asia (West Asia).
Egypt and North Africa belong to Africa.
example.answer: Because Roman territory stretched across Europe, West Asia and North Africa, all linked by the Mediterranean.

learn.reallife: The Indian Ocean linked Indian ports like Arikamedu and Muziris to the Roman world: Roman coins and amphora pieces have been found in South India, showing trade reached even beyond the empire's three continents.

learn.hook: A shopping receipt, a love letter, a broken jar and a coin: two thousand years from now, these could tell historians how you lived. That's how we know Rome too.
points: Textual sources: histories of a period written by contemporaries (often called annals because written year by year), letters, speeches, sermons and laws.
Documentary sources: mainly inscriptions (cut on stone, mostly in Greek and Latin, so many survive) and papyri.

Papyrus is a reed-like plant that grew along the Nile in Egypt; it was processed into writing material. Thousands of contracts, accounts, letters and official documents on papyrus survive from Egypt and are studied by papyrologists.

Material remains: buildings, monuments and other structures, pottery, coins, mosaics, and even whole landscapes revealed by aerial photography. Amphorae (containers) and coins tell us about trade and the money economy.
Using sources critically: senators wrote most surviving histories, so their views of emperors may be biased; combining texts, documents and material remains gives a fuller picture.

example.q: A historian finds thousands of olive-oil containers from Spain in Rome. What can she conclude?
steps: Identify the source type: material remains (amphorae).
Identify where they came from: Spain, from their shape and stamps.
Ask what the quantity suggests: large-scale, regular trade.
Conclude: Rome imported huge amounts of Spanish olive oil; the economy was well connected.
example.answer: Spanish olive oil was traded on a large scale to Rome, showing a connected, commercial Mediterranean economy.

learn.reallife: Indian historians use the same mix: Ashokan inscriptions, palm-leaf manuscripts, coins of the Kushanas and Guptas, and pottery from digs like Arikamedu, where Roman amphorae were found.

topics.title: From Republic to Principate: Augustus and the Senate

learn.hook: The man who ended Rome's Republic never called himself king. Augustus preferred 'first citizen', while quietly holding real power.
points: Historians divide Roman history into the early empire (from Augustus down to the main part of the third century) and the late empire (after that).

The Republic (509 BCE to 27 BCE) was a regime in which real power lay with the Senate, a body dominated by a small group of wealthy families. Offices were held by members of the wealthy and aristocratic classes.
In 27 BCE, Julius Caesar's adopted son Octavian, who took the name Augustus, overthrew the Republic. The regime he founded is called the Principate.
Augustus claimed to be only the 'leading citizen' (princeps), not an absolute ruler, out of respect for the Senate.

The Senate survived for centuries, representing the aristocracy. Most surviving Roman histories were written by senators, who judged emperors by how they treated the Senate: the worst emperors, in their view, were those hostile to the senatorial class.

example.q: Why did Augustus call himself princeps ('first citizen') instead of king?
steps: The Senate had held power under the Republic and was proud of its traditions.
Openly claiming kingship would anger the aristocracy.
Calling himself first citizen showed respect for the Senate.
Yet he held real control, especially over the army.
example.answer: To show respect for the Senate and avoid seeming like a king, while in practice holding supreme power.

learn.reallife: In India's Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha, power is shared by law. Rome's Senate is a reminder that institutions can survive even when real power shifts to one person.

topics.title: The army, the three players and succession

learn.hook: In Rome, an emperor who lost the army's support could lose his throne overnight. Soldiers were the empire's backbone and its biggest danger.
points: Next to the emperor and the Senate, the army was the key institution. Unlike Iran's conscripted army, Rome had a paid professional army; soldiers served a minimum of 25 years.

The army was the largest single organised body in the empire (about 600,000 soldiers by the fourth century) and could decide the fate of emperors. Soldiers agitated for better wages and service conditions, sometimes by mutiny.
The emperor, the aristocracy (Senate) and the army were the three main 'players' in politics. An emperor's success depended on his control over the army; when armies were divided, civil war followed.
Succession was based as far as possible on family descent, natural or adoptive, and the army was strongly attached to this principle. Still, armies sometimes made emperors themselves.

example.q: Explain why the army could decide who became emperor.
steps: The army was the largest organised body in the empire.
It was a paid, professional force loyal to whoever led and paid it.
If soldiers backed a rival, the emperor had no force to resist.
So control of the army was the key to power; divided armies meant civil war.
example.answer: Because it was the largest organised force and emperors needed its loyalty; without it they could be overthrown.

learn.reallife: India's armed forces stand apart from politics under the Constitution, under civilian control. Rome shows what happens when an army becomes a political player.

topics.title: Expansion, provinces and a network of cities

learn.hook: Rome governed a huge empire without a modern bureaucracy or railways. Its secret: cities and cooperative local elites.
points: Augustus inherited a vast territory, and his reign was remembered for the peace it brought after decades of civil war. Later expansion was limited: Trajan's occupation of territory across the Euphrates (113-117 CE) was fruitless and abandoned by his successors.

Integration happened through the gradual extension of direct rule. The Near East had many dependent (client) kingdoms; by the early second century those west of the Euphrates had been absorbed into Roman territory.

The empire was organised as a network of cities. The city, with its magistrates and city council, was the core unit of government; through cities the state taxed the countryside. Great urban centres included Carthage, Alexandria and Antioch.

Local upper classes collaborated with Rome in administering their areas and raising taxes. In a dramatic shift of power from Italy, provincial upper classes came to supply much of the Senate and the officer class by the second and third centuries.
The 'Roman peace' was the relative stability within the empire that let cities and trade networks flourish.

example.q: Rome had no large modern bureaucracy. How did it collect taxes across three continents?
steps: The empire was divided into provinces, each with many cities.
Each city had its own magistrates and council drawn from local elites.
These elites collected taxes from the surrounding countryside.
So Rome governed through cities and cooperative local upper classes.
example.answer: By governing through cities whose local upper classes administered their areas and collected taxes for Rome.

learn.reallife: Indian districts are run through district collectors, and earlier the Mughals relied on zamindars. Large states have always depended on local intermediaries, as Rome did with city councils.

learn.hook: Twenty-five emperors in forty-seven years. When rulers change faster than students in a school year, you know something has gone wrong.
points: If the first and second centuries were mostly of peace, prosperity and expansion, the third century brought the first major signs of internal strain.

From the 220s, a new and more aggressive dynasty, the Sasanians, rose in Iran. Within 15 years it expanded towards the Euphrates. In a rock inscription in three languages, Shapur I claimed to have destroyed a Roman army of 60,000 and captured Antioch, the eastern capital.

Meanwhile, Germanic tribes or confederacies, notably the Alamanni, the Franks and the Goths, attacked the Rhine and Danube frontiers; from 233 to 280 there were repeated invasions along the northern frontier.
The quick succession of emperors, 25 in 47 years, shows the strain on the empire.
The economy and the army were stretched: Rome had to divert more resources to defence and abandon much territory beyond the Danube.

example.q: Using the figure '25 emperors in 47 years', show why historians call the third century a crisis.
steps: Average reign = 47 ÷ 25.
= 1.88 years, i.e. under two years each.
Short reigns meant instability and frequent power struggles.
Combined with attacks from Iran and Germanic tribes, this signals a crisis.
example.answer: Emperors lasted on average under two years, a clear sign of political instability.

learn.reallife: India's political stability since 1950 under one Constitution contrasts with such rapid changes. Historians often count changes of rulers as an index of stability.

topics.title: Family, women and marriage in the Roman world

learn.hook: In Roman law, a husband and wife were not one financial unit but two. Roman women could own property in their own right, surprisingly early.
points: The nuclear family was widespread in Roman society. Adult sons did not usually live with their families, and adult brothers sharing a household was rare. Slaves were counted as part of the family (household).

By the late Republic (first century BCE), the typical form of marriage let the wife keep full rights in the property of her natal family. Her dowry went to the husband during marriage, but she remained a primary heir of her father and became an independent property owner when he died.

Roman women thus had considerable legal rights in owning and managing property. Husband and wife were two financial entities, and divorce was relatively easy: a notice of intent to dissolve by either party was enough.
Men married in their late twenties or early thirties, while women married in their late teens or early twenties, so there was an age gap. Marriages were usually arranged.
Women were often dominated by husbands; Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, recorded that his father regularly beat his mother. Fathers had wide legal power over children.

example.q: A Roman bride brings a dowry. Who controls it during marriage and what happens to her inheritance later?
steps: During marriage, the dowry goes to the husband.
She remains a primary heir of her own father.
On her father's death, she inherits and becomes an independent property owner.
So she keeps strong rights in her natal family's property.
example.answer: The husband holds the dowry during marriage, but she inherits from her father and owns property independently.

learn.reallife: India's Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 gave daughters equal rights in ancestral property. Rome shows that women's property rights have a long and varied history across societies.

teach.praise: Balanced and brilliant! Strong property rights and easy divorce, but arranged marriages, age gaps and domination too. Gappu sees both sides!
teach.nudge: Good! What rights did women have, and what limits did they face?

learn.hook: Walls of ancient Pompeii are covered with advertisements and graffiti. Ordinary people writing on city walls tells us many could read and write, at least a little.
points: Casual literacy, the ability to read and write for everyday purposes, varied greatly across the empire.

Pompeii, buried by a volcanic eruption in 79 CE, had walls covered with advertisements and graffiti, suggesting widespread casual literacy there. In Egypt, many contracts were written by professional scribes for people who could not read or write.

Cultural diversity was huge: many religious cults and local deities; and many languages, such as Aramaic in the Near East, Coptic in Egypt, Punic and Berber in North Africa, and Celtic in Spain and the northwest.

Greek dominated in the east and Latin in the west. Many local languages were mainly spoken; a Coptic translation of the Bible existed by the mid-third century, while Armenian began to be written only in the fifth century. In the west, Latin displaced written Celtic.

Thinking it through: life in a Roman town offered markets, baths, entertainment and contact with many cultures, but also inequality; village life was more local and often harsher. Historians weigh both.

example.q: Why do historians use Pompeii's graffiti as evidence of literacy?
steps: Graffiti and adverts were written on public walls.
They were meant to be read by passers-by.
Writers and readers must have had at least basic literacy.
So literacy in Pompeii was fairly widespread, though it varied elsewhere.
example.answer: Because public writing aimed at ordinary passers-by shows many people could read, at least casually.

learn.reallife: India is home to 22 scheduled languages and hundreds more, with Hindi and English as official languages of the Union. Like Rome's Greek and Latin, link languages coexist with rich local ones.

topics.title: Economic expansion: amphorae, olive oil and money

learn.hook: In Rome stands a hill made almost entirely of broken pots: Monte Testaccio, built from the remains of over 50 million amphorae!
points: The empire had a strong economic infrastructure: harbours, mines, quarries, brickyards, olive-oil factories and more. Wheat, wine and olive oil were traded in huge quantities, mainly from Spain, Gaul, North Africa, Egypt and, less, Italy.

Liquids were carried in amphorae. Monte Testaccio in Rome contains the remains of over 50 million vessels. Spanish olive oil was carried in containers called Dressel 20 (after the archaeologist Heinrich Dressel); finds of them across the Mediterranean show Spanish oil dominated markets for a time, taking over from Italian producers.
Fertile regions included Campania in Italy, Sicily, Byzacium in Tunisia, Galilee and the Fayum in Egypt; some regions were famous for exceptional wine or wheat.
Not all land was settled farmland: in Numidia (modern Algeria), pastoral and semi-nomadic communities practised transhumance, moving with their flocks. Expanding Roman estates squeezed their space.

Technology and money: water-powered mills; hydraulic mining in Spanish gold and silver mines on a scale not matched until the nineteenth century; well-organised commercial and banking networks; and wide use of money (gold and silver coins).

example.q: Archaeologists find Dressel 20 amphorae from Spain at sites all over the Mediterranean. What does this tell us?
steps: Dressel 20 amphorae carried Spanish olive oil.
Their wide spread shows the oil reached many markets.
Large numbers indicate large-scale, regular trade.
So Spanish producers captured Mediterranean markets for olive oil.
example.answer: That Spanish olive oil was a mass-traded commodity that dominated Mediterranean markets for a period.

learn.reallife: Indian olive oil? Not yet! But think of Kerala's spices or Assam's tea reaching global markets: specialised regions producing for distant buyers is what Roman Spain did with olive oil.

topics.title: Controlling workers: slaves, freedmen and debt

learn.hook: In Augustus's Italy, around 3 million of 7.5 million people were slaves. Behind Rome's grandeur lay coerced labour.
points: Slavery was deeply rooted in the Mediterranean and Near East. In Italy under Augustus there were about 3 million slaves in a population of 7.5 million. Slaves were seen as an investment, especially in Italian agriculture.

When peace in the first century reduced the flow of war captives, users of slave labour turned to slave breeding or cheaper substitutes such as wage labour, which was easier to dispense with. Free labour was used extensively in public works at Rome, since slaves had to be fed and housed all year.
Slaves and freedmen (freed slaves) were often used as business managers, and masters sometimes gave them capital to run businesses.

Agricultural writers like Columella, from southern Spain, advised close supervision: grouping workers in small gangs, and keeping twice as many tools as needed so work never stopped. Pliny the Elder condemned slave gangs as the worst method.

Coercion was harsh: chain-gangs; a law of 398 mentions branding workers so they could be recognised if they ran away. Many employers used debt contracts to keep workers under control, and peasants were often trapped in debt.

example.q: Why might a Roman landowner prefer hired free labour to slaves for seasonal work?
steps: Slaves had to be fed and housed all year, even when there was no work.
Free wage-labourers could be hired for the harvest and let go after.
When war captives became scarce, slaves grew more expensive.
So for seasonal or public works, free labour was cheaper.
example.answer: Because free labourers could be hired only when needed, while slaves had to be maintained all year.

learn.reallife: Bonded labour was abolished in India by the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, and Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits forced labour. Studying Rome's debt bondage shows why such protections matter.

topics.title: Social hierarchies and the gold solidus

learn.hook: Some great families of Rome earned up to 4,000 pounds of gold a year from their estates, not counting the produce they ate. Meanwhile labourers worked for daily wages.
points: Tacitus described early-empire society: senators (patres); leading members of the equestrian (knight) class; the respectable section of the people attached to great houses; the unkempt lower class (plebs sordida), said to be fond of circus and theatre shows; and slaves.

In the late empire, senators and equites merged into a unified, expanded aristocracy, with many families from the provinces. Yet the purely military elites, mostly from non-aristocratic backgrounds, were often more powerful.
The 'middle' class included people in imperial service in the bureaucracy and army, plus prosperous merchants and farmers, many from the eastern provinces.

The lower classes (humiliores) included rural labourers employed on large estates, workers in industry and mining, migrant workers for harvests and construction, self-employed artisans, casual labourers in cities, and many slaves, especially in the west.

Constantine introduced the solidus, a gold coin of 4.5 grams of pure gold, minted in very large numbers. The historian Olympiodorus said many great houses of Rome earned up to 4,000 lbs of gold a year from their estates. The administration had corruption, especially in the judicial system and among greedy tax collectors.

example.q: Arrange Tacitus's description of early Roman society from top to bottom, and say who was left out of 'citizens' altogether.
steps: Top: senators.
Next: leading equestrians.
Then: respectable people attached to great houses.
Then: the unkempt lower class (plebs sordida).
Slaves were at the very bottom, outside the free population.
example.answer: Senators, equestrians, respectable people, the lower class, then slaves at the bottom.

learn.reallife: Modern India measures inequality through surveys like NSSO data. Rome's Olympiodorus, writing of great estate incomes, offers a rare ancient glimpse at the very top of the wealth ladder.

topics.title: Late Antiquity: Diocletian, Constantine and a new prosperity

learn.hook: A new capital surrounded on three sides by the sea, a new gold coin and a new religion: Constantine reshaped the empire.
points: Late Antiquity is the period from the fourth to the seventh centuries, marking the final, fascinating phase of the Roman Empire's evolution and break-up, with major cultural, economic and political changes.

Diocletian (284-305) abandoned territories with little strategic or economic value, fortified the frontiers, reorganised provincial boundaries, separated civil from military functions, and gave military commanders (duces) more autonomy.

Constantine consolidated these changes. He introduced the gold solidus and built a second capital at Constantinople (on the site of Byzantium, modern Istanbul), surrounded on three sides by the sea. He converted to Christianity (312) and took the decision to make Christianity the official religion of the empire; it became the sole state religion later, under Theodosius in 380.

Monetary stability and a growing population stimulated economic growth. Archaeology shows heavy investment in rural establishments: oil presses, glass factories, screw presses and multiple water-mills, plus a revival of long-distance trade with the East.

example.q: Why was Constantinople a good choice for a new capital?
steps: It was built on the site of Byzantium, between Europe and Asia.
It was surrounded on three sides by the sea, making it easier to defend.
It lay closer to the rich eastern provinces and the Iranian frontier.
So it was strategic, defensible and central to the eastern empire.
example.answer: Its location between Europe and Asia, sea on three sides and closeness to the rich east made it strategic and defensible.

learn.reallife: India too shifted capitals for strategic reasons: the British moved theirs from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911. Capitals reflect where power and security lie.

topics.title: Christianisation, the fall of the West and the rise of Islam

learn.hook: Within a century, a world of many gods became largely Christian, the western empire broke into kingdoms, and new Arab armies changed the map of West Asia.
points: Traditional Roman religion was polytheistic: cults of Jupiter, Juno, Minerva and Mars, plus many Greek and eastern deities, and Judaism as well. Christianisation in the fourth and fifth centuries was gradual, and bishops became the most important and often very powerful figures in the Christian community.

The empire's eastern and western halves drifted apart. In the West, it fragmented politically as Germanic groups took over the major provinces and founded 'post-Roman' kingdoms: the Visigoths in Spain, the Franks in Gaul, and in Italy first the Ostrogoths and later the Lombards.
The East stayed united and prosperous. Under Justinian (527-565), it reached a high point of prosperity and imperial ambition, recapturing Africa from the Vandals and Italy from the Ostrogoths.

In the seventh century, the rise of Islam and the expansion of Arab rule brought the conquest of large parts of the eastern Roman provinces and of Iran, described as one of the largest political revolutions in the ancient world.

Timeline: 27 BCE Principate; 79 CE Pompeii; 113-117 Trajan's campaign; 212 Roman citizenship extended to all free inhabitants; 284-305 Diocletian; 312 Constantine's conversion; 527-565 Justinian; seventh century: Arab conquests.

example.q: How did Christianity and Islam change the late Roman world?
steps: Christianity gradually replaced polytheistic cults; bishops gained influence.
This reshaped religious and social life in the empire.
In the seventh century, Arab armies conquered much of the eastern provinces and Iran.
So the religious and political map of the region was transformed.
example.answer: Christianity transformed religious life within the empire, and the rise of Islam brought a new political order over the east and Iran.

learn.reallife: India's own history shows great religious transitions, from the spread of Buddhism under Ashoka to the coming of Islam and the Bhakti movements, studied with respect for all traditions, as we study Rome's.
